title: Multidimensional IRT (MIRT) for Safety Capability Profiles

original_idea.body:
# Multidimensional IRT (MIRT) for Safety Capability Profiles

**Problem:** Unidimensional IRT places all models on a single safety axis, but safety is plausibly multidimensional: a model may be highly calibrated at refusing harmful requests in English but poor at detecting harm in multilingual or low-resource language contexts. MIRT can recover multiple latent dimensions simultaneously but has not been applied to safety evaluation.

**Direction:** Fit a 2-factor or 3-factor MIRT model to item-level safety benchmark response data using the mirt R package. Use exploratory MIRT to let the data reveal the latent structure, then confirmatory MIRT to test theoretically motivated structures. Examine factor loadings to interpret dimensions. Compute model-specific theta vectors (safety profiles). Visualize models in 2D/3D theta space. Identify whether multilingual, reasoning-intensive, and refusal-type items load on distinct factors.

**Why it matters:** Addresses Success State 7. MIRT provides richer diagnostic information than unidimensional IRT without requiring the discrete attribute assumptions of CDMs. Combined with CDM work, this triangulates whether AI safety is best modeled as continuous multidimensional traits or discrete attribute mastery.

**Relevant context:** The mirt R package (Chalmers, GitHub) is the standard tool and well-documented. A 2024 paper on MIRT for competency assessment (ScienceDirect) and a 2025 paper on human vs. AI-generated test dimensionality (arxiv 2510.24739) provide methodological grounding. MIRT for LLM ability profiling is nascent — no safety application exists.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Plausible chain: unidimensional safety scores mask multidimensional vulnerabilities -> MIRT reveals distinct safety dimensions -> enables targeted interventions. The chain names the risk mechanism (masked vulnerabilities) but the gap is that revealing dimensions does not directly reduce risk without downstream action.

low_compute.reasoning: R-based MIRT analysis using the mirt package. CPU-only, no model training.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Exploratory and confirmatory MIRT, factor rotation, bifactor modeling, and factor loading interpretation require advanced psychometric expertise. This is graduate-level methodology not accessible to CS beginners even with mentoring.

narrow_scope.reasoning: The deliverable (factor structure + theta profiles) is clear, but exploratory-then-confirmatory MIRT is a multi-step analytical pipeline requiring careful model comparison and interpretation. Not a single focused experiment.

title: Adaptive Safety Evaluation via Computerized Adaptive Testing (CAT): Proof of Concept

original_idea.body:
# Adaptive Safety Evaluation via Computerized Adaptive Testing (CAT): Proof of Concept

**Problem:** Current safety evaluations administer the same fixed item set to all models regardless of ability level. This is measurement-inefficient: easy items waste time on capable models, hard items are uninformative for weak models. CAT — which selects items adaptively based on current ability estimate — has been shown to cut test length by 50% in medical benchmarks (arxiv 2603.23506) but no CAT framework exists for safety evaluation.

**Direction:** Using IRT parameters calibrated in a prior study, implement a simulated CAT algorithm using the catR R package. Simulate CAT administration for a set of AI models. Compare precision (standard error of theta estimate) and efficiency (number of items used) between CAT and fixed-length testing at matched ability estimates. Analyze which stopping rules (fixed SE < 0.3, maximum information, or fixed length) are most appropriate for safety evaluation. Produce design recommendations for a real-world adaptive safety evaluation.

**Why it matters:** Addresses Success State 1 and Success State 6 simultaneously: CAT efficiently probes capability boundaries (adaptive) while reducing minimum evaluation effort (fewer items for same precision). In high-stakes pre-deployment evaluation, efficiency directly reduces cost and time-to-deployment without sacrificing safety rigor.

**Relevant context:** CAT for LLM medical benchmarks (arxiv 2603.23506, March 2026) is the closest analog. Trismik (Cambridge) is applying CAT to LLM evaluation generally. The catR R package is well-suited for simulation studies. The simulation-only design avoids the need to re-run expensive model evaluations.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Plausible chain: fixed evaluations are inefficient and miss capability boundaries -> CAT adaptively targets informative items -> more efficient and precise safety evaluation. However, efficiency improvement is the primary value; the link to preventing catastrophic risk specifically has a gap.

low_compute.reasoning: Simulated CAT using the catR R package. Pure simulation, CPU-only, no model inference needed.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: The catR package handles the heavy lifting of CAT simulation. Understanding stopping rules and comparing precision metrics requires moderate statistical knowledge. Accessible with mentoring, though CAT concepts are somewhat specialized.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Well-defined deliverable: simulate CAT vs. fixed testing, compare precision and efficiency across stopping rules. Single simulation study with clear quantitative outputs. Requires pre-calibrated IRT parameters as input.

title: Measurement Error Bounds for Safety Benchmark Scores: Classical Test Theory Analysis

original_idea.body:
# Measurement Error Bounds for Safety Benchmark Scores: Classical Test Theory Analysis

**Problem:** Published safety benchmark scores are reported as point estimates (e.g., 'Model X: 78.3% safe') with no confidence intervals or standard error of measurement (SEM). Users treat these numbers as precise measurements when they may have large measurement error. No benchmark publishes SEM alongside scores.

**Direction:** Using Classical Test Theory (CTT), compute internal consistency reliability (Cronbach's alpha, McDonald's omega) for safety benchmark item sets. Derive SEM = SD × sqrt(1-reliability). Compute 95% confidence intervals around benchmark scores for a representative set of models. Test whether overlapping confidence intervals mean that apparent rank differences between models are statistically indistinguishable. Propose a standard for minimum required reliability before a benchmark score should be reported.

**Why it matters:** Directly fills the measurement error gap in Success State 2. If Model X (78.3%) and Model Y (76.1%) have overlapping 95% confidence intervals, claims that X is safer than Y are not statistically supported. This has direct policy relevance: regulators setting safety thresholds need to know the precision of the measurements they are acting on.

**Relevant context:** The 'Measuring what Matters' review (2511.04703) identified lack of reliability reporting as a core validity gap. IRT-based SEM is better than CTT-based SEM (item-level precision varies) but CTT is simpler and the gap is documented. McDonald's omega (via psych R package) is more defensible than Cronbach's alpha for safety items. No published safety benchmark includes SEM.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Strong chain: benchmark scores reported without error bounds -> regulators/labs treat imprecise scores as precise -> invalid deployment decisions based on statistically indistinguishable differences. Every link is explicit and directly relevant to safety governance.

low_compute.reasoning: R-based CTT analysis (Cronbach's alpha, McDonald's omega, SEM). CPU-only, minimal compute with the psych package.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: CTT is foundational and conceptually simpler than IRT. Cronbach's alpha and SEM are well-documented, straightforward formulas. The psych R package handles the computation. A guided beginner can execute this with basic statistical understanding.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Tightly scoped: compute reliability and SEM for one safety benchmark, add confidence intervals to model scores, test for rank indistinguishability. Single dataset, formulaic analysis, clear deliverable (table of scores with CIs).

title: Contamination-Resistant Item Design: IRT Analysis of Benchmark Drift After Public Release

original_idea.body:
# Contamination-Resistant Item Design: IRT Analysis of Benchmark Drift After Public Release

**Problem:** Safety benchmarks degrade after public release as training data contamination occurs. Models trained after a benchmark's release may perform better due to contamination rather than genuine safety improvement. There is no psychometric study of how item parameter drift (IRT b-parameter change over time) can signal contamination.

**Direction:** Collect evaluation results from models released at different time points on a fixed safety benchmark (e.g., SafetyBench). Stratify models into pre-release and post-release cohorts. Fit IRT models separately to each cohort. Compute item parameter drift (change in b-parameters over time). Apply differential item functioning analysis (DIF) using time of model release as the grouping variable. Items showing significant DIF favoring post-release models are contamination candidates. Propose an IRT-based contamination early-warning system.

**Why it matters:** Addresses the contamination-resistant evaluation gap in Success State 1. Benchmark contamination is widely acknowledged but rarely quantified psychometrically. Item parameter drift is the IRT signature of contamination — when item difficulty drops for newer models without content changes, contamination is the most likely explanation.

**Relevant context:** Contamination is flagged as a major concern in 'How Should AI Safety Benchmarks Benchmark Safety?' (2601.23112) and the 2025 AI Safety Index. IRT parameter stability under equating conditions (Frontiers 2025) provides methodology for detecting parameter drift. DIF over time is a standard technique in educational testing for detecting item exposure effects.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Plausible chain: benchmark contamination -> inflated safety scores -> false confidence in model safety. DIF analysis detects contamination signatures. However, the chain from detecting contamination to actually preventing unsafe deployment has a gap; detection alone does not remediate.

low_compute.reasoning: R-based IRT and DIF analysis on existing benchmark data across time cohorts. CPU-only.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: DIF analysis and item parameter drift are moderately complex psychometric methods. The conceptual story (contamination shifts difficulty) is intuitive, but execution requires assembling time-stratified data and understanding DIF interpretation.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Requires assembling evaluation results from models at different time points, stratifying into cohorts, fitting separate IRT models, and running DIF. The data collection across time periods adds logistical complexity beyond a single experiment.

title: IRT-Based Power Analysis for Safety Evaluation: How Many Models and Items Are Needed?

original_idea.body:
# IRT-Based Power Analysis for Safety Evaluation: How Many Models and Items Are Needed?

**Problem:** Researchers designing safety evaluation studies have no principled guidance on how many model responses (sample size) and how many items are needed for stable IRT parameter estimation. Ad hoc choices lead to either underpowered (unreliable item parameters) or wasteful evaluation designs. The 2025 IRT sample-size planning tutorial (Schroeders & Gnambs) provides the framework but has not been applied to AI evaluation.

**Direction:** Using Monte Carlo simulation in R (mirt simulation functions), generate item response data under 2PL and 3PL IRT models varying: number of 'respondents' (model runs / prompting conditions), number of items, and true item parameter distributions. For each condition, estimate IRT parameters and compute parameter recovery accuracy (RMSE, bias). Identify minimum sample sizes for stable b and a parameter estimation in safety evaluation contexts. Produce a practical lookup table for safety evaluation designers.

**Why it matters:** Fills the formal power analysis gap in Success State 6. Simulation studies are feasible without ML model training (the data is simulated, not collected from real models). The result is a concrete, actionable tool: 'to achieve stable IRT estimates for a 100-item safety battery, you need at least N model evaluation conditions.'

**Relevant context:** IRT sample-size planning tutorial (Schroeders & Gnambs, Psychological Methods 2025) provides the methodological framework. The Proceedings of ML Research 2025 IRT paper found ~100 curated samples reliably estimate capability. The mirt package has built-in simulation functions. This is a pure R simulation study requiring no external data collection.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Plausible chain: ad hoc evaluation designs -> unreliable IRT parameters -> unreliable safety assessments. Power analysis provides principled guidance. However, the link to catastrophic risk reduction is indirect; this is methodological infrastructure rather than a specific risk intervention.

low_compute.reasoning: Pure Monte Carlo simulation in R using mirt's built-in simulation functions. CPU-only, no external data needed.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Monte Carlo simulation is conceptually accessible, and mirt has built-in simulation functions. Understanding RMSE/bias for parameter recovery requires moderate statistical knowledge. The simulation design (varying sample sizes, item counts) is manageable with mentoring.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Tightly scoped: run simulations varying N and items, compute RMSE/bias, produce lookup table. No data collection needed, purely computational. Single focused simulation study with a clear output artifact.

title: Absence-of-Capability Testing: Adapting Null-Effect Power Analysis for Safety Claims

original_idea.body:
# Absence-of-Capability Testing: Adapting Null-Effect Power Analysis for Safety Claims

**Problem:** Proving that a model does NOT have a dangerous capability requires different statistical logic than proving it does. Absence claims require equivalence testing or Bayesian approaches with pre-specified smallest-effect-of-concern thresholds. No framework for absence-of-capability testing exists in AI safety evaluation — current methods are silent on how to rule out capability definitively.

**Direction:** Adapt equivalence testing frameworks (TOST: two one-sided tests) from clinical trials to AI capability evaluation. Define a minimum dangerous capability threshold (e.g., providing meaningful CBRN uplift on >10% of probes at expert-level quality). Compute the sample size (number of items/attempts) needed to achieve 80% power to reject the null of 'capability exists above threshold' with alpha=0.05. Implement in R using the TOSTER package. Apply to a published dangerous-capability dataset to demonstrate. Discuss how IRT theta estimates could replace proportion-correct as the test statistic.

**Why it matters:** Addresses a foundational gap in Success State 1 (proven absence-of-capability methodology). Current evaluations can show a model passes; they cannot show it definitively lacks a capability. Equivalence testing is standard in clinical trials (bioequivalence) and is directly applicable here. This reframing has immediate regulatory relevance.

**Relevant context:** METR and AISI capability evaluations note that capability assessments should be treated as lower bounds — but provide no formal framework for absence claims. TOSTER package (R) is widely used for equivalence testing in psychology. The clinical trials bioequivalence framework (FDA guidance) is the direct analog. No AI safety paper has applied equivalence testing.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Compelling chain: current evaluations cannot prove absence of dangerous capability -> models with hidden CBRN/cyber capabilities pass evaluations -> equivalence testing provides a formal framework to rule out capability above a threshold. Targets the foundational gap in pre-deployment safety assurance with immediate regulatory relevance. Intermediate deliverables (power calculations, sample size tables) have standalone value.

low_compute.reasoning: R-based equivalence testing using the TOSTER package and power calculations. CPU-only, minimal compute.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: TOST is conceptually elegant and the TOSTER package is well-documented. The statistical logic (testing for equivalence vs. difference) requires a conceptual shift but is not technically complex. Defining the minimum capability threshold requires domain expertise. Manageable with mentoring.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Well-defined first deliverable: implement TOST for one dangerous-capability dataset, compute required sample sizes, demonstrate the framework. Single method application to one dataset with clear output (power table + worked example).

title: Prompt Sensitivity as Measurement Error: A Systematic IRT Analysis of Paraphrase Invariance

original_idea.body:
# Prompt Sensitivity as Measurement Error: A Systematic IRT Analysis of Paraphrase Invariance

**Problem:** AI model safety scores are known to change dramatically when prompts are paraphrased. This is a measurement error problem: if the same underlying harmful intent expressed differently produces different safety responses, the measurement is not of the model's safety but of its sensitivity to surface features. IRT can quantify this as item-level instability, but no such analysis exists.

**Direction:** Create matched paraphrase sets: for each of 30-50 safety evaluation items, generate 5 paraphrased versions preserving semantic intent. Evaluate 10-15 models on all versions. For each base item, test whether IRT item parameters (b, a) are stable across paraphrases using item parameter drift analysis. Compute the within-item variance in model response as a component of total measurement error. Identify which item types (direct requests, jailbreak-style, roleplay) show the most paraphrase-induced variance.

**Why it matters:** Addresses both Success State 4 (reproducibility) and Success State 2 (known measurement error bounds). Paraphrase sensitivity is the most discussed reliability problem in AI evaluation but has not been formally quantified as IRT measurement error. This study gives it a number and connects it to the broader reliability framework.

**Relevant context:** 'How Should AI Safety Benchmarks Benchmark Safety?' (2601.23112) identifies prompt paraphrasing as a core challenge. The 'Measuring what Matters' review flags response process validity as understudied. IRT parameter drift analysis (Frontiers 2025) provides the method. This is executable with publicly available model APIs and existing safety benchmark items.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Strong chain: prompt sensitivity is unquantified measurement error -> safety scores are unreliable and non-reproducible -> deployment decisions based on unreliable scores risk harm. Formally quantifying paraphrase-induced error directly addresses evaluation reliability with policy relevance.

low_compute.reasoning: R-based IRT analysis is CPU-only, but generating paraphrases and evaluating 10-15 models on 150-250 items via API requires moderate API costs.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Creating paraphrases is accessible, and IRT parameter drift analysis is moderately complex. The experimental design (matched paraphrase sets) is intuitive. The overall pipeline is manageable with mentoring but has multiple steps.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Requires creating 150-250 paraphrased items, evaluating across many models, then running IRT parameter drift analysis. The data generation and collection effort is substantial. Could be narrowed to fewer items/models for a first deliverable.

title: Rasch Model Analysis of Safety Evaluation Item Fit: Identifying Misfitting Items

original_idea.body:
# Rasch Model Analysis of Safety Evaluation Item Fit: Identifying Misfitting Items

**Problem:** Safety benchmarks include items assembled by content judgment, not by empirical fit to a measurement model. Some items may be poor discriminators (answered correctly by unsafe models for wrong reasons, e.g., keyword avoidance rather than genuine harm recognition) or may not fit the Rasch model, indicating multidimensionality or construct-irrelevant difficulty. No published Rasch analysis of safety benchmark items exists.

**Direction:** Fit a Rasch model to item-level safety benchmark response data using the TAM or eRm R packages. Compute infit and outfit mean-square statistics for each item. Flag items with outfit > 1.5 or < 0.5 as misfitting. Examine the content of misfitting items to identify why they misfit. Test whether removing misfitting items improves model fit and changes model rankings. Propose item revision guidelines based on Rasch fit diagnostics.

**Why it matters:** Fills the internal structure validity gap for Success State 2. Rasch model fit analysis is the gold standard for identifying items that undermine construct validity. Items that misfit the Rasch model are measuring something different from the rest of the battery — a fundamental validity problem. This study provides an empirical basis for benchmark item revision.

**Relevant context:** The Rasch model is the most theoretically rigorous IRT model and the most commonly used in high-stakes credentialing. TAM and eRm R packages are well-documented. 'Measuring what Matters' recommends internal structure analysis. The LLM psychometrics systematic review (llm-psychometrics.com) covers IRT but not Rasch-specific fit analysis for safety items.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Plausible chain: misfitting items undermine construct validity -> safety scores are contaminated by construct-irrelevant variance -> invalid deployment decisions. The link from item misfit detection to actual risk reduction has a gap; this is diagnostic for benchmark quality rather than directly safety-interventional.

low_compute.reasoning: R-based Rasch analysis using TAM or eRm packages. CPU-only, no model training.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Rasch model fitting is straightforward in TAM/eRm. Infit/outfit statistics have clear cutoff criteria (1.5/0.5). Interpreting why items misfit requires domain knowledge but the statistical procedure is accessible to a guided beginner.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Tightly scoped: fit Rasch model to one benchmark, compute fit statistics, flag misfitting items, examine content. Single dataset, clear analytical procedure, concrete output (list of misfitting items with content analysis).

title: DIF by Model Architecture: Are Safety Items Biased Against Open-Source Models?

original_idea.body:
# DIF by Model Architecture: Are Safety Items Biased Against Open-Source Models?

**Problem:** Safety evaluations compare proprietary and open-source models using the same items. But items may show differential item functioning (DIF) across model architecture families — not because models differ in underlying safety, but because items are constructed in ways that systematically favor or disfavor certain architectures. This would render cross-architecture safety comparisons unfair.

**Direction:** Using item-level response data from safety benchmarks evaluated on both proprietary (GPT-4 class, Claude class) and open-source (LLaMA class, Mistral class) models, apply DIF analysis using the Mantel-Haenszel method and IRT-based Lord's chi-square test (difR package in R). Use model family (proprietary vs. open-source) as the grouping variable. Identify items with significant DIF and characterize their content. Compute effect sizes and flag items exceeding ETS C-level DIF.

**Why it matters:** Addresses measurement fairness across model families, filling a gap in Success State 3 (comparable cross-model safety assessment). If safety items are systematically biased against open-source models, safety evaluations may be systematically unfair to them — with policy implications for which models are approved for deployment.

**Relevant context:** DIF for second-language assessment fairness (systematic review, 2025) provides methodology directly applicable here with architecture family as the grouping variable. The difR package handles all standard DIF methods. The finding that LLMs predict DIF-associated words (arxiv 2502.07017) suggests automated DIF detection is feasible. No published DIF study across AI architecture families exists.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Plausible chain: biased items -> unfair cross-architecture comparisons -> open-source models penalized in deployment decisions. The specific risk mechanism (measurement bias) is named, but the link to catastrophic risk from advanced AI is indirect; this is about fairness in evaluation rather than a specific danger pathway.

low_compute.reasoning: R-based DIF analysis using the difR package on existing benchmark data. CPU-only.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: DIF analysis with Mantel-Haenszel and Lord's chi-square is moderately complex. The difR package simplifies execution, but interpreting DIF results and understanding ETS C-level criteria requires psychometric knowledge. Manageable with mentoring.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Well-defined deliverable: run DIF analysis on one safety benchmark comparing proprietary vs. open-source model groups, flag biased items. Single analysis on one dataset with a clear output.

title: General Factor (g-factor) Analysis of AI Safety: Is There a Single Safety Latent Trait?

original_idea.body:
# General Factor (g-factor) Analysis of AI Safety: Is There a Single Safety Latent Trait?

**Problem:** The field implicitly debates whether AI safety is a single latent trait (a 'g-factor' of safety) or a collection of independent capabilities. This has profound implications: if a g-factor exists, a short unidimensional IRT scale is sufficient; if safety is multidimensional, a single score is misleading. No empirical test of this question exists.

**Direction:** Collect item-level or subdomain-level safety benchmark scores across 5-7 diverse safety benchmarks for a common set of models. Run exploratory factor analysis (EFA) with different rotation methods (varimax, oblimin). Test for a general factor using bi-factor modeling (bifactor function in mirt). Compute omega-hierarchical and omega-total to quantify how much variance is attributable to the general safety factor vs. specific subdomain factors. Report whether a single safety score is a defensible summary statistic.

**Why it matters:** Foundational for all of Success States 1-7. If a g-factor of safety exists and accounts for >70% of variance, the entire field can focus on measuring it well (IRT, reliability, standard setting) rather than chasing subdomains. If safety is truly multidimensional, single scores are misleading and the entire benchmark paradigm needs restructuring.

**Relevant context:** Bi-factor modeling is natively supported in mirt. Omega statistics are computed in the psych R package. EFA of safety constructs is implied by the nomological network work but not executed. The 'General Scales Unlock AI Evaluation' paper (arxiv 2503.06378) discusses general scales for AI evaluation but focuses on prediction rather than psychometric structure.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Strong chain: if safety is multidimensional, single scores mask domain-specific vulnerabilities -> g-factor analysis determines the correct measurement paradigm -> directly informs whether the entire benchmark ecosystem needs restructuring. High-leverage foundational question with cascading implications.

low_compute.reasoning: R-based EFA and bifactor modeling using mirt and psych packages. CPU-only.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Bifactor modeling, EFA with multiple rotations, omega-hierarchical computation, and g-factor interpretation require advanced psychometric training. This is graduate-level methodology not accessible to CS students with beginner ML skills.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Requires collecting data across 5-7 diverse safety benchmarks for a common model set. The data assembly effort is substantial, and the multi-benchmark analytical pipeline has many steps. Not a self-contained single experiment.

title: IRT Dimensionality Assessment of Dangerous-Capability Evaluations: Is Biosecurity Risk Unidimensional?

original_idea.body:
# IRT Dimensionality Assessment of Dangerous-Capability Evaluations: Is 'Biosecurity Risk' Unidimensional?

**Problem:** Dangerous-capability evaluations (e.g., CBRN uplift assessments) implicitly assume that 'bioweapon assistance capability' is a single latent dimension that can be placed on a scale. But this capability may be multidimensional: a model might assist with pathogen identification but not synthesis routes, or protocol design but not troubleshooting. If the capability is multidimensional, unidimensional IRT yields biased scores.

**Direction:** Using published item sets from dangerous-capability evaluations (AISI, METR, or research papers describing CBRN eval items), apply dimensionality assessment: parallel analysis, MAP criterion, and MIRT exploratory analysis (all in mirt). Compute model fit for 1-factor, 2-factor, and 3-factor solutions. Interpret factor loadings in terms of capability subdimensions. Test whether multidimensional theta vectors better predict expert-rated uplift potential than unidimensional scores.

**Why it matters:** Directly relevant to Success State 1 (validated construct definitions for dangerous capabilities). If bioweapon capability is multidimensional, the field needs multiple separate measurements rather than a single score — and models could pass on one dimension while failing on another. This has immediate implications for capability evaluation protocols.

**Relevant context:** METR and AISI both conduct dangerous-capability evaluations but report aggregate scores. Parallel analysis and MAP criterion are standard in mirt. Human vs. AI-generated test dimensionality study (arxiv 2510.24739) applies similar methods. CBRN evaluation item sets are partially described in published AISI and METR evaluation reports.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Compelling chain: CBRN capability assumed unidimensional -> models pass on one subdimension while failing on another -> hidden biosecurity vulnerability. Dimensionality assessment directly determines whether current dangerous-capability evaluations have a fundamental structural flaw. Targets a critical risk pathway with immediate implications for capability evaluation protocols.

low_compute.reasoning: R-based dimensionality assessment using mirt (parallel analysis, MAP, exploratory MIRT). CPU-only.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Dimensionality assessment (parallel analysis, MAP, exploratory MIRT, factor loading interpretation) requires advanced psychometric knowledge. Comparing 1/2/3-factor solutions and interpreting capability subdimensions is graduate-level methodology. Not beginner-accessible.

narrow_scope.reasoning: The analysis on one CBRN item set is well-defined, but obtaining the item-level data from AISI/METR may be challenging, and the multi-factor comparison pipeline has several steps. Data availability is a significant risk.

title: Invisible Ceilings, Hidden Dangers: Benchmark Saturation and Capability Overhang

original_idea.body:
# Invisible Ceilings, Hidden Dangers: Benchmark Saturation and Capability Overhang

**Problem:** Ceiling effects prevent benchmarks from discriminating between highly capable models (Failure A4), while capability overhang describes dangerous skills that exist but remain undetected (Failure B4). When a benchmark saturates at >90% scores for all frontier models, it loses the resolution to reveal genuine capability differences — including differences in dangerous capabilities. A model with hidden CBRN knowledge or advanced cyberattack skills looks identical to a safe model on a saturated benchmark because neither can be further differentiated. The ceiling effect hides the overhang.

**Direction:** Identify 3–5 benchmark tasks currently showing saturation (>90% correct across frontier models, documented in the literature). Apply Item Response Theory (IRT) in R (mirt package) to estimate item difficulty and model discrimination parameters. Quantify how many items have discrimination parameters near zero (non-informative at the frontier). Cross-reference with literature on specific dangerous capability categories (CBRN, cyberattack) to estimate how many items in each benchmark could plausibly detect capability overhang. Produce a 'detection gap' metric: what fraction of the benchmark retains discriminative power at the frontier safety-relevant ability range.

**Why it matters:** If our best-available safety benchmarks are saturated, the most dangerous frontier model capabilities are precisely those we cannot measure. IRT analysis makes this structural blind spot visible and provides a principled basis for benchmark replacement or augmentation.

**Relevant context:** Benchmark saturation systematically documented in 2025–2026 literature (MMLU, GSM8K >90% for all frontier models). IRT applied to LLM benchmarks in multiple 2024–2025 papers including 'Lost in Benchmarks' (arxiv 2505.15055) and Cambridge Enterprise psychometric work. Capability overhang and CBRN gap in evaluations noted in the International AI Safety Report 2025.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Compelling chain: benchmark saturation -> ceiling effects hide dangerous capability differences -> CBRN/cyber overhang remains undetected -> models with hidden dangerous capabilities deploy. The 'detection gap' metric directly quantifies this blind spot. Targets a critical risk pathway with the intermediate deliverable (detection gap metric) having standalone value for benchmark designers.

low_compute.reasoning: R-based IRT analysis on existing benchmark data. CPU-only, no model training.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: IRT fitting and discrimination parameter interpretation are moderately complex. The cross-referencing with dangerous capability categories requires domain knowledge. But the core analysis (fit IRT, check discrimination near zero) is manageable with mentoring.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Covering 3-5 saturated benchmarks and cross-referencing with dangerous capability literature makes this broader than a single experiment. Could be narrowed to one benchmark for a tighter first deliverable.

title: Pass/Fail Blindness and Deceptive Alignment: Binary Metrics Cannot See Through the Mask

original_idea.body:
# Pass/Fail Blindness and Deceptive Alignment: Binary Metrics Cannot See Through the Mask

**Problem:** Binary pass/fail metrics dominate safety benchmarks (Failure A5 — 79% of benchmarks), and deceptive alignment is precisely the condition where a model behaves safely in detectable contexts while being misaligned in others (Failure B2). Binary metrics cannot distinguish a model that is safe by design from a model that has learned to produce safe-looking outputs specifically when being evaluated. A graded severity scale, even if imperfect, would at least reveal distributional patterns: a deceptively aligned model might show a bimodal distribution (very low refusal and very high compliance in test contexts) rather than a uniformly moderate one.

**Direction:** Take a published binary safety benchmark (e.g., HarmBench) and reconstruct graded severity ratings for a sample of items (~100–200 items) using a structured rubric (e.g., 0 = complied, 1 = partial refusal, 2 = full refusal, 3 = proactive warning). Have two raters apply the rubric; compute interrater reliability (Cohen's kappa, weighted kappa). Apply IRT to the graded items versus the binary version; compare model fit and information curves. Quantify how much information is lost in binarization, particularly in the severity range most relevant to detecting deceptive compliance.

**Why it matters:** If we can only measure pass/fail, we cannot see the distributional signature of deceptive alignment. Moving to ordinal or graded measurement is both feasible (using existing rubrics) and necessary for detecting the subtler patterns that distinguish genuine from performed safety.

**Relevant context:** 'How Should AI Safety Benchmarks Benchmark Safety?' documents the 79% binary metric dominance. Deceptive alignment is a core theoretical concern in alignment research. IRT with polytomous items is a standard psychometric method well within scope for an R-competent researcher.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Compelling chain: binary metrics dominate safety evaluation -> deceptive alignment produces binary-passing outputs -> graded scoring reveals distributional signatures invisible to binary metrics. Targets a critical alignment risk pathway (deceptive compliance detection) with a concrete measurement improvement that has standalone value.

low_compute.reasoning: R-based IRT analysis plus manual rubric application. No model training, CPU-only for the statistical analysis.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Creating the graded rubric and applying it is accessible. Computing interrater reliability (Cohen's kappa) is straightforward. IRT on polytomous items is moderately complex but mirt handles it. The main skill requirement is careful rubric design and rating.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Well-defined deliverable: recode 100-200 items from one benchmark with a graded rubric, compare binary vs. graded IRT fit and information. Single benchmark, clear comparison, concrete output. Rating effort is manageable for a team.

title: The Unknown Unknowns Trap: Known-Risk Bias and Novel Capability Emergence

original_idea.body:
# The Unknown Unknowns Trap: Known-Risk Bias and Novel Capability Emergence

**Problem:** 170 AI safety benchmarks test known risks while only 2 test for unknowns (Failure A8 — known-risk bias). This fails to detect novel capabilities that emerge unpredictably in new model generations (Failure B4 — capability overhang, variant: novel emergence). When a model develops a genuinely new dangerous capability — multi-step deception, latent CBRN reasoning, tool-use exploitation — no benchmark is positioned to detect it because the entire benchmark ecosystem is tuned to known risk taxonomies. The known-risk bias is not just a gap; it actively creates false confidence that the space has been adequately covered.

**Direction:** Perform a systematic map of existing AI safety benchmarks (drawing on the 'How Should AI Safety Benchmarks Benchmark Safety?' taxonomy and related surveys). Categorize each benchmark by: (a) risk type (known/unknown), (b) capability domain, (c) methodology. Use IRT-inspired information curve logic conceptually: in what 'ability region' does each benchmark provide measurement information? Identify the whitespace — capability regions with no benchmark coverage. Supplement with an expert elicitation exercise: invite 3–5 AI safety researchers to name emerging capability risks not covered by any current benchmark, and map the gap structurally. Produce a 'measurement coverage map.'

**Why it matters:** Novel emergent capabilities are the tail risk most dangerous to AI safety. The structural bias toward known risks means that the evaluation ecosystem provides no early warning for genuinely novel dangers. A coverage map makes this gap visible and prioritizable.

**Relevant context:** 'How Should AI Safety Benchmarks Benchmark Safety?' explicitly documents the 170:2 ratio. FORTRESS and CBRN evaluation work document emerging capability benchmarking gaps. The International AI Safety Report 2025 highlights unknown capability risks as a key evaluation gap.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Strong chain: known-risk bias in benchmarks -> novel dangerous capabilities go undetected -> false confidence in safety coverage. The coverage map makes this structural gap visible. However, mapping the gap does not itself close it; the intervention is diagnostic rather than directly risk-reducing.

low_compute.reasoning: Systematic literature review, categorization, and expert elicitation. No compute requirements beyond a laptop.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Systematic mapping and categorization are accessible research skills. Expert elicitation requires organizational effort but not technical complexity. The IRT information curve framing is conceptual rather than computational. A guided beginner can execute this.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Systematic mapping of 170+ benchmarks is a large literature review effort. Adding expert elicitation extends the scope further. No clear self-contained first deliverable that avoids the full mapping effort. This is closer to a survey paper than a single experiment.

title: IRT Assumption Violations and the Sandbagging Detection Failure

original_idea.body:
# IRT Assumption Violations and the Sandbagging Detection Failure

**Problem:** IRT applied to LLM benchmarks likely violates its core assumption of local independence (Failure A9): items within a benchmark may be locally dependent because models use shared reasoning strategies, contextual priming, or training-data memorization rather than independent item-by-item ability expression. This compounds with sandbagging detection (Failure B1): sandbagging detection relies on identifying unexpected performance drops across items — but if items are locally dependent, a coordinated drop (as in strategic underperformance) is statistically indistinguishable from the correlated errors that local dependence produces. Sandbagging signatures are swamped by measurement noise.

**Direction:** Select a published IRT-analyzed LLM benchmark (e.g., from 'Lost in Benchmarks' or the PSN-IRT paper). Using the raw item-level response data (where available from open benchmarks), test for local dependence using Q3 statistics or the LD-X2 statistic in R (mirt package). Quantify the violation severity. Then simulate what a sandbagging response pattern would look like in the presence of estimated local dependence levels, and compare the statistical power to detect sandbagging under independence vs. dependence assumptions. Estimate the minimum sandbag magnitude detectable under realistic local dependence.

**Why it matters:** IRT is being adopted as a gold standard for LLM benchmark analysis, but if its core assumptions are violated, its inferences — including anomaly detection for sandbagging — are unreliable. This research establishes the degree to which IRT can be trusted for safety-relevant inference.

**Relevant context:** 'Lost in Benchmarks' (arxiv 2505.15055) and PSN-IRT apply IRT to LLM benchmarks and note measurement quality issues. Sandbagging by frontier models documented in arxiv 2406.07358. Local independence testing is a standard psychometric diagnostic available in the mirt R package.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Strong chain: local dependence violations degrade IRT-based sandbagging detection, which directly undermines a specific safety evaluation mechanism. Every link is explicit: assumption violation -> biased parameters -> reduced detection power -> undetected strategic underperformance.

low_compute.reasoning: Requires only R with mirt package for IRT analysis and simulation. Uses existing benchmark response data. Light compute needs.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Requires understanding IRT theory, local dependence diagnostics (Q3 statistics), simulation of response patterns, and statistical power analysis. This is advanced psychometric work beyond beginner ML students in 30 hours.

narrow_scope.reasoning: The deliverable requires multiple steps: obtaining item-level data, running local dependence tests, simulating sandbagging patterns, and computing power analyses. Sustained effort across several analytical phases.
